posts.title: Ask HN: If AI tools are so good, why isn't your bug backlog empty?
posts.text: A lot of people outside tech ask me if AI is going to replace programmers and I just think: if that were the case we should be running out of things to do The bug backlog should be empty and we've caught up to every feature request from PMs to the point that we are bottlenecked on the business side But that does not seem to be the case with my own company or most devs I talk to in the industry So what gives?

comments.text: I don't know if I'm doing something wrong but bug fixing with AI has always been a crapshoot. You can absolutely tell an agent to fix an issue, and it will fix that issue, but the vast majority of the time that solution will be by adding code to cover the specific symptom in the bug report. It rarely considers or recommends solutions that have tradeoffs that may change behavior but will eliminate an entire class of similar bugs. This is mostly a problem of agents not having the autonomy of managing an entire project and having the ability to make tradeoffs to increase simplicity or maintainability, but when given that autonomy no AI model I've used uses that privilege to write simpler, more maintainable code.
comments.author: frostiness

comments.text: All my solo project backlogs _are_ empty. For my team projects, I still need my teammates to review code, so that bottlenecks how quickly we can burn down the backlog. If I didn't need code review I would have the backlog burned down in weeks, but I'd create a bunch of outages in the process (we do catch things in code review!) Also, some of my solo projects are gamedev-related, and gamedev is also bottlenecked on actually playing your game to see if its fun :) but it is great to get out of a 2 hour playtest session with notes and have a new build in like 15 minutes with the feedback incorporated.
comments.author: td521534f12

comments.text: It pretty much is? Every easily-described bug has been fixed. The only things that remain are "this isn't wrong per se, it just violates customer expectations" and someone needs to figure out what the product should do in this case. We burnt through our backlog of "obviously we should do this when we have time" stuff in the spring. It was pretty fun to kill pretty much all of my multi-year refactor and cleanup list. Now we are pretty much bottlenecked on the business side.
comments.author: fishtoaster

comments.text: For my personal projects: 4 have zero backlog of any sort. 1 has a fleet of agents working through some product improvements that I postponed until the very end of the project. It's a very rote "rebuild this game on a modern engine" project to resurrect a game I developed 20 years ago, and there's a few small improvements I want to make to the game that deviate from the original. Today is day 5 of the rebuild, so it's not exactly a long-lived project per se -- but the bots did identify a bunch of defects in the original game and addressed them as part of the conversion project. 1 has: - A few flaky tests to clean up. - A couple heisenbugs that I can't pin down until I get a couple PCs for testing (3D graphics stuff is Fun<tm>). - A whole lot of features that consist of one sentence I wrote down to avoid losing track of an idea, and which I may or may not ultimately choose to implement at all. - A couple issues that can't proceed until a human gets involved. I.E. I need to go through the hassle of setting up a corporation and setting up accounts with the various gate keepers (Apple, Google, Valve). The biggest bottlenecks for me, at this moment are -- in descending order: 1. Running the linters / test suites / build processes for two of my projects completely slam my machine (load average hit 290 earlier today with 3 agents running things across the 2 game dev projects; CircleCI / Github Actions would be waaaay too expensive so I'm running it all locally until I can set up a CI runner node). 2. My bandwidth for acceptance testing, and other human-only work (read: game balance / play experience) 3. Weekly usage caps for fixed-price plans from the three services I use. Setting aside my relatively unusual circumstances: At any business, you're going to have a problem of information rot when it comes to a backlog. The person who recorded a defect or feature request may not remember enough context to make it actionable (or they may not be at the org anymore). The assumptions underpinning the issue may or may not hold anymore (and it may not be clear which situation you're in). Etc. Plus, there's going to be a not-unreasonable risk aversion to making changes that are in peripheral areas of the system that don't get a lot of attention -- lest fixing one issue cause some unexpected but undesirable outcome. A lot of it mostly boils down to either "institutional knowledge gap" or "acceptance testing is a bottleneck".
comments.author: jfrisby

comments.text: Because AI is better at finding bugs than at fixing them. It is not good at writing bug-free code either. AI and humans don't make the same bugs. So AI may find bugs that are easily overlooked by humans while at the same time being incredibly stupid on some other parts.
comments.author: GuB-42

comments.text: > The bug backlog should be empty I don't follow. Maybe it's just me, but I've never worked at a company and on any substantial product that had an empty bug backlog. If a bug queue is empty, the product is either not used much (or not a priority), not tested well enough, or not monitored enough. I don't know that a world where AI has mostly replaced programmers is a world with an empty bug queue. While AI is reducing the _quantity_ of programmers needed in many cases, it is also an output multiplier for the remaining programmers, while often raising the bug-to-code ratio. AI has led to more output, more projects, and more bugs.
comments.author: yokuze

comments.text: If your team and product had a large backlog before thats not going to change. AI tools amplify whatever it is you do so if you've been ignoring bugs and focusing most of the time on new features, AI isn't going to magically change what a team is working on. On a technical level, take your average NullPointerException or the equivalent in whatever language you use. Ask AI to go fix it and it will sanely wrap or check for nulls in that piece of code. Ask a lead or senior engineer to fix it and they will (hopefully) start with "why is this data null? it shouldn't be" and then trace back through logs or data, try to recreate with a real scenario and not only fix that bug but find there's an unhandled scenario somewhere else in the code base. Someone could prompt the AI to expand further and do a root cause analysis but do you trust it to find things and fix them properly?
comments.author: mattbrewsbytes

comments.text: I'm not a big fan of AI, but we are expected to use it at my job. In my position, it wouldn't really matter how good AI is, because when we find a bug it will often take an hour long meeting, or even multiple meetings, just to figure out what a given behavior should actually be before we can even attempt to fix it.

comments.text: AI only can improve velocity if it mostly works unsupervised. But most people don't trust their agents to run alone. And to build that trust will take some time, people will need to learn how to use AI effectively. I think the PS3 hardware could be a good analogy. It was really powerful, but nobody really knew how to use it. After a few years people got really good at it . And you can view this evolution by the improvement of graphical fidelity we got over the years.

comments.text: The perfect app is like crafting dorodango. You make smaller and smaller changes, and use finer tools. AI is not a fine tool. It's one of the earlier stages of the crafting process. It's like a block of marble, roughly in the form of your sculpture, but you must continue to remove from it. But if you're making rough bricks instead of fine art, then it's a perfectly decent tool.

comments.text: Parkinson's Law: "Work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkinson%27s_Law

comments.text: I'm in devops, not programming, so slightly different. I can say our backlog of absolutely essential jobs that we haven't been able to get around to for the last 5 years is absolutely being smashed out one by one. A lot of this is unattended server migrations running over night being validated the next day. The backlog as a whole though is growing as we have AI continually probing the infrastructure and various code bases looking for new security concerns or ways to improve performance and save money. Directly as a result of this, our cloud costs dropped massively in the last 6 months with only very minimal impact on performance. I absolutely see a time in the not too distant future where all our infrastructure tech debt has been cleaned up, the security situation is as good as we can get it, the backlog has completely emptied and some of my team will be surplus to requirements.

comments.text: There's a chicken and egg story here as well: AI speeds up everything so the amount of code written is much higher, which does still contain bugs, even if AI can mostly solve them as well, new code will keep being written as well... That doesn't mean AI tools aren't good, but obviously they aren't perfect either. Luckily...

comments.text: I think building new code up to a functional, code and security standard will get easier and easier with AI and we may reach a point where the list of bugs is shorter. However, based on what I have seen building my software factory (7 agents, each with their own roles) and iterating on it, an agent will only have a certain amount of context and scrutiny it can dedicate. So I found that segregation of resonsibilities between agents (which one does which checks) + automated checks and tests are really important. However, I don't know yet to what extent. It feels like my factory is getting better and better, but there are still things being sent back, and still there is an occasional helper that is getting re-written a bit differently (even if I have a tech lead agent who is looking at the whole code). So I can only imagine the complexity for a legacy app or a huge app where even multiple agents cannot have enough context to write code that considers code and functions next to the feature it is working on. I don't think that agents at this time can have the capability of a senior dev who really knows the system. The best thing we can do is to distill how a senior dev looks at the system from all different angles and write instructions as clear and short as possible. Then iterate and test continuously with measuring the outcomes. At least that's what I'm trying to do.

comments.text: We're living out the consequences of not having updated the security models of our operating systems since the Internet was commercialized and became a persistent connection on most computers. They can't ever be made secure unless you want to go back to disconnected PCs with only floppy drives that had hardware write protection and no other persistent storage. This is a hell of our own choosing, and was entirely preventable. It can be fixed, but doing so will make fixing Y2K look like a picnic because everything is going to have to be redone. Everything currently running needs to be isolated in a VM at a minimum.

posts.title: Ask HN: Anyone else blurting?
posts.text: Like most, I was stoked on LLMs when they became available. Particularly on the earlier free tiers where the slightly questionable answers were offset by generous tokens. Now, I'm finding that having to use this tech is becoming much less fun. The constant corrections, the constant prompting for greater brevity, the grating certainty and sycophancy. Others probably are forgiving considering the net benefit. But for me it honestly now feels like a chore, which is reflected in how my frustration is now appearing in how I communicate to it now. Instead of articulating and making my prompts precise, I'm just straight-out blurting. Typos, missed words, poor semantic structure - I guess I maybe at some point reasoned that "it will get the picture, so why waste effort being articulate?" Or maybe I'm just anticipating that it is going to get it 15 percent wrong, so why even try and be articulate. Just blurt and steer. Blurt and steer. Is anyone else finding this? I actually sometimes worry about it. I feel it's not just the fact that I'm offloading my cognition to it that is making me dumber, it is the way I'm communicating with it. They say the act of writing is tied to the act of thinking, and my prompts are basicslly the typographic equivalent of grunting right now.

comments.text: I do. Maybe not terribly but quite a bit. And for all the same reasons as yours :) Although this happens less frequently with Chinese models, and recently Gemini Argon with medium level thinking. Anthropic and OpenAI appear to have defined success as number of prompts sent or number of assistant responses, which means more work for me, so I am out. Plus, I wouldn’t talk to someone twice if they caveat every answer to a question and require me to follow up. I don’t ask questions expecting partial answers with exactly 1 caveat/nuance.
comments.author: ozozozd

comments.text: It's poor form. You're lifting from your back. You're throwing punches from your elbow. You shouldn't anticipate that it will get 15% off and steer. You try to get it up to 100% before writing any code, and sometimes that involves getting it to scout what's already there. Control the environment. The scope used to be code and architecture, now it's context. These models are designed to fill in gaps and propose solutions. If they don't know what you want, you have productivity in the the wrong direction. If you want somewhere to start, look into Matt Pocock's public videos and https://www.aihero.dev/ A rule of thumb would be to speak to it like a teacher would. It has always worked on all models.
comments.author: muzani

posts.title: Ask HN: Are the more software malfunctions now than before?
posts.text: I have the feeling (reading HN every day for the past 15 years) that the amount of major software malfunctions has increased drastically over the last year, maybe two. I remember that back in 2016-17 big failure events (cloud outages, critical infrastructure issues etc) were special discussion topics. Today they feel more like a routine event. If you also believe it's the case, what could be the reason? Cultural shift towards software? Global load increase? AI slop?

comments.text: Dependency between products has increased a lot. I've been maintaining web applications since the early 2000s, back then if your server was ok, your site was ok, period. Now if any of {AWS, github CI, cloudflare, google cloud, claude, microsoft, a dozen auth providers, etc} is down, your application is surely going down.

It's primary purpose is for live boxscores because all of the major sports sites have terrible UI/UX experiences. I always defaulted to ESPN.com but it's so slow and awful. Center Court is basically a bridge between espn.com (or nba.com) and more advanced stat focused sites that don't offer a good live experience. Instead of storing computed statistics in a database, I store raw play by play payloads immutability and everything else is derived from those and can be trivially rebuilt so the event log is a derived cache of the payloads. Every stat on every page is a pure fold over the event log at request time; no derived number is stored. This enables some powerful features like being able to re-derive a game's entire state at any point of the game (or even a time range). comments.text: I'm still back at the question of what goals we are trying to achieve in the first place. Much of the software dev industry jumped straight to "automating coding is the goal", and I haven't yet agreed with that conclusion. Speeding it up? Sure. Doing the tedious work, implementing known algorithms, sure. Finding your way around unfamiliar codebases, yes. We could list more - there are plenty of great use cases, and I partake of them. But the biggest value I have ever seen offered by individuals in the software industry comes in the form of institutional knowledge. The kind that allows some of us to hear about a few odd symptoms, think it through in our head, and immediately narrow down the problem space we need to troubleshoot into something small and manageable. Or can hear about a potential refactor and spit out a quick list of impacts it would have to the system in a few minutes on a call. Can LLMs do that? Maybe. Should they? I'm not so sure. If they can do in seconds what a human can do in days/weeks, that is clearly valuable. If they do in seconds what a human can do in minutes, that is less valuable. I lean towards a belief that human holders of the knowledge is a good thing, but LLMs could absolutely assist with knowledge transfer and sharing, making even more people able to work at that level. I'm simply unconvinced that outsourcing all that to LLMs is desirable. I am 100% convinced that massive amounts of work, efforts, infrastructure build-out, and money could get LLMs to that point. But my question remains because that same level of resources could also do so many other things for our society. So I'm not stuck on "What could LLMs do?", I'm stuck on "What society do we want to live in?", and not at all convinced that the AI-pilled "AI can do it all" world is desired, even if it is possible.

posts.title: Tell HN: HN is being scraped for emails to scam
posts.text: I know that many folks here post their personal emails in the Who's for Hire monthly pages and other places, and want to remind you that this public site gets views from folks with ill intent (or their bots/agents) as well. I use unique emails for every site, so I immediately knew that the late AWS payments email sent to my HN email were fake. There were other tells, but I want to remind everyone to be vigilant! HN is public but even social media sites where you supposedly can make your page private I've had some of those emails suddenly have spam sent to as well. Please be safe everyone! My favorite tells that an email is a scam: - Before opening a surprising/suspicious email, hover over the sender name to see the domain the sender came from (don't open the email if it's strange). - _If_ you already opened the email, before clicking any links in the email, hover over them to see the domain that the link sends you to. There are dozens more tips but a full article would be required, and these two will prevent you from falling for nearly all of them.

posts.title: Ask HN: Do you still enjoy coding in C++?
posts.text: In the recent years C++ received a lot of backlash due to its complexity and (perceived) feature creep. However, since C++11 I really enjoyed writing C++ with its strict type system (including const), range-based for loops, smart pointers, and how much you can do with templates. On the other hand, I know that it can be very tricky to write, for instance, a correct iterator, to get handling of rvalue references right, or to read error messages that involve templates. So, do you enjoy or dislike writing C++ source code and why?

comments.text: Oh, C++. C++ feels like an old lover who I think fondly of. We were together many years, until about C++20, through thick and thin. It was exhilarating - blazingly fast, perhaps irresponsibly so, but heck, the ride was wild. It taught me so many things, and shaped me into the programmer I am today. But we went our separate ways when its shortcomings became too large to bear, and its behavior - too often undefined - no longer excusable. I keep up with it because I still have love for it, but I have to admit I am deeply concerned about many of the life choices it is making. I should have seen how problematic it was, because I knew its history, but I had hope that it could change, and it just looks like it never will. I'm still rooting for C++, even though I am very happy with my new primary language, Rust. I hope it changes to the better, because I really want the best for it, but right now I'm just not seeing it. It keeps repeating old mistakes (e.g., more UB footguns with every new feature), without addressing any of the big flaws (insufficient tools for building robust software). I sometimes still write C++, but I'm not excited about it the way I used to be. When I do write C++, it's because I have to. When given the choice, Rust is simply just a better choice for almost everything I do. Right now, I don't see a future for C++ and me.
comments.author: simonask

comments.text: I'm really torn about C++. I love C++ but there are things that I really don't like about it as well. It's a fantastic language in a lot of ways, but it carries around 40+ years of cruft, of things that you wouldn't do like that if you were inventing a programming language today. I haven't written C++ professionally for many years at this point, and my memories of using it professionally (pre C++ 11) are not happy ones: having to agree on a strict subset of the language that we were allowed to use, which avoided features that any of the compilers didn't support well, or that my teammates didn't like. Sadly back then the list of forbidden features included templates and namespaces. But using C++ on personal projects nowadays, and being able to choose which bits of the language to use - and which to avoid - is much more enjoyable. And honestly, the language did get a lot better from C++ 11 onwards.
comments.author: chris_j

comments.text: In one word: Power. C++ is by far the most powerful language around. And this is for the best and (often) also the worst. In term of generic programming, control on hardware, capacity of abstraction and more generally expressivity: Nothing, even today, come even close to C++. It is a language full of foot guns and it has its fair share of legacy problems. But if you learn to avoid it (throught experience and pain). You can reach a productivity and a level of performance in C++ which is very difficult to beat with anything else, including Rust. Ironically, I find it particularly true in the age of A.I. Because the amount of C++ around is so tremendous, that agents are currently pretty good at it if guided properly.

I think Rust is a better language in many ways and I think it's the future of low-level programming (and I think it's wild that it took so many decades to get a proper competitor to C++!). But I also like how C++ doesn't care and lets me do whatever I want without acting as a nanny. I would never ever dare to write a publicly exposed web server in C++, but a game? Sure!

comments.text: I love C++, in the C++11 days I even organized a local C++ User Group at my university, and I've used it for the last 20 years as my main language. I still appreciate its many merits but since a bit more than a year I migrated to Rust and I find it very difficult to look back, except for maintaining my previous C++ projects. Surprisingly, it's not Rust's memory safety features that I miss the most when turning back to C++. It's mostly the absence of algebraic data types and pattern matching, and the split between compile-time and runtime polymorphism, i.e. concepts vs virtual classes, where in Rust you just have traits and use them for everything. On top of that the tooling and the ecosystem are just amazing. There's a proposal for pattern matching sitting there under the committee's desk for some years now. With the mess that the standard committee is going through I really doubt they will be able to ship pattern matching for C++29 or even later. Too little too late. So to answer the question, yes, I still appreciate the merits of C++ but I don't enjoy writing it as much as I have in the past.

comments.text: Personally, I've never seen anyone write C++ codebases without boost. As you pointed out, the only practical way seems to be to constraint its feature complexity through meta programming. Coming from the embedded C++ world where resources are scarce, C++ and its debugger ecosystem have been really nice. There were usually strong vendor provided SDKs and cross compilation toolchains available. The issues I had with the language were mostly dependencies on vendors, not effectively being able to fix problems in SDKs, and as you also mentioned the footguns. Lots of frustrations came from codestyle, branch conventions and type conventions we tried to encode into templates, which new team members had to learn before they could write any production code. So from a team perspective a lot of productivity came from reproducible build pipelines and setups. Having one team member on Windows and the other on macOS or Linux was as painful as it can get, especially with getting gcc's ecosystem to work properly. So you were also really dependent on Docker cross architecture images. And setting those up just for the sake of compilation was also unnecessary overhead. These days I've migrated towards Go for pretty much all tasks I can think of, mostly for the tight integration with the C ABI ecosystem and tinygo and the easy possibility to cross compile into fat binaries. What I miss though is a "real IDE" like the old Visual Studio, or geany or whatever. Most IDEs are not symbol based anymore, which makes them really painful to use in terms of what I expect an IDE to offer to be able to call itself an IDE. But maybe this is just my C++ heart bleeding all over the place because I miss good and typed API documentation examples that I can explore through clicking rather than having to google every function all the time.
